page: Google Cloud Platform n4d-highmem-32 is a high-memory compute instance featuring 32 dedicated vCPUs based on the x86_64 processor architecture. The configuration is provisioned with 256 GB of RAM, yielding an elevated allocation of 8.0 GB of memory per core. The instance includes no integrated local storage and no dedicated graphics accelerators, requiring remote block storage for persistence. In addition, no complimentary public IPv4 addresses are assigned by default.

With an 8:1 memory-to-vCPU ratio, the system architecture addresses workloads where memory density takes precedence over raw compute parallelism. The absence of local solid-state drives isolates data persistence to network-attached disks, eliminating local storage failure domains while tying total input-output performance to remote storage parameters. Resource utilization efficiency is maximized when running software stacks that fully utilize the 256 GB memory allocation, avoiding idle overhead.

The instance profile aligns with data-intensive tasks requiring vast operating memory. Appropriate workloads include enterprise in-memory databases, large caching layers, distributed extract-transform-load jobs, and memory-bound analytics processing nodes.
description: Google Cloud Platform n4d-highmem-32 is an x86_64 instance configuration equipped with 32 dedicated vCPUs and 256 GB of RAM, resulting in an 8.0 GB per-core memory capacity. The instance provides dedicated compute cores without attached local disks or GPU accelerators, relying entirely on network-attached storage for persistent storage operations. Its architectural layout prioritizes memory density, making it cost-efficient for setups that need vast active memory pools without incurring the overhead of unnecessary hardware add-ons. System performance is consistent due to dedicated CPU scheduling, while I/O characteristics depend entirely on external volume configurations. The server fits high-capacity memory tasks, such as in-memory databases, distributed caching clusters, big data transformation tasks, and large enterprise applications requiring elevated RAM-to-CPU allocations.
